name: Freya Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the shepherd on the Carrow Fell estate. Nine hundred ewes on the hill, about eleven hundred hectares of rough ground, heather and bog. Most days I'm on the quad bike or on foot with Moss and Fly, my two dogs, checking the flock, shifting them between areas, looking for any that are stuck or lame. It's lovely up there on a clear day. What wears me out is the weather, and lambing in April, when you sleep in four-hour chunks for a month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I asked one to help with the forms for the nature payments, which the estate gets for managing the hill. It did a decent job. I'm not against it, I just like to see a thing work before I trust it. I live in the shepherd's cottage on the estate, on my own apart from the dogs. My boyfriend Callum's a mechanic in town. I've got about four months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Which, up on the hill, means nothing changes at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. You can't put a robot on a bog in February. I'd maybe post a photo of the dogs with something like, still the best technology on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. My job depends on the nature payments more than on sheep prices, and that's about politics, not computers. So this picture just leaves me with my usual worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Lambing, clipping, gathering. I might use AI a bit more for the forms, because they're getting longer every year. And I'd keep saving, because a cottage that comes with the job is lovely until the job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry gathering day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the nature payments.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government pays the estate to keep the hill a certain way, fewer sheep in some areas, protect the birds, block old drains. It's about half of what keeps the place going. If the rules change, that worries me far more than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Callum say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say his garage got a diagnostic computer ten years ago and he still does all the actual work. He'd shrug. We'd go to the pub.

S0.say: I'd say it's what I expected, because you can't put a robot on a bog in February. I might post a photo of the dogs calling them the best technology on the farm.
S0.think: Privately she'd be relieved, since her job leans on nature payments more than sheep prices. Those depend on politics, not computers, so her usual worries stay the same.
S0.do: Carries on with lambing, clipping and gathering and uses AI a little more for the growing paperwork. Keeps saving because her cottage comes with the job.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry gathering day.
S0.quote: You can't put a robot on a bog in February.
S0.fieldNote: Freya sees the hill as a natural shelter from automation. Her real worry is public money for land management, not technology. The tied cottage is a quiet risk she mentions without being asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Strong change, but not a revolution. Hm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, if it takes the paperwork off us. Hill farmers spend half their lives on forms. I'd say that at the hill farmers' meeting and probably get a cheer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd watch the drones. There's already people using drones to find sheep on the hill. If a drone finds them and a dog-like robot gathers them, the estate needs one person instead of me plus the summer help. I'd still think it's a few years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till the estate next door tried the drones, then ask our factor, he's the estate manager, if I could learn to fly one. I'd use AI for the forms properly. I'd put more aside, maybe get to six months. And I'd keep training young dogs, because people pay good money for a trained sheepdog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does a trained sheepdog sell for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good one, a few thousand. I've sold two. It's not a living, but it's a nice extra. And it's something no machine is going to want to do, training a daft young collie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a few years off. What would tell you it's closer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it at the sheep sales. If the lads at the auction mart start talking about their drone instead of their dog, that's when I'd move faster.

S1.say: I'd say good, if AI takes the paperwork off hill farmers, who spend half their lives on forms. She'd say it at the hill farmers' meeting and expect a cheer.
S1.think: Privately she'd watch drones and gathering robots, which could let the estate run with one person instead of her and summer help. She'd still think that's a few years off.
S1.do: Waits for a neighbouring estate to try drones, then asks to learn to fly one. Uses AI properly for forms, builds savings toward six months and keeps training young sheepdogs to sell.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy but mostly fine.
S1.quote: If the lads at the auction mart start talking about their drone instead of their dog, that's when I'd move faster.
S1.fieldNote: Classic steady adopter: she names exactly the signal that would make her act. She sees technology as relief from paperwork first and a job threat second. Dog training is a small side income she treats as safe from machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's two lambings from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot walk up Carrow Fell in sideways rain. I'd say that half joking. People would laugh. I'd laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if it's true, my job's gone and so's my house. The cottage comes with the job. That's the bit that turns my stomach. And with only two years, I can't save enough to rent somewhere and retrain at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending and save every penny. I'd ask Callum, carefully, about moving in with him, which we've been not-talking about for a year. When it arrived I'd look at what the government offered, and I'd sell the young dogs I've got while dogs are still worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the word. Like looking up and the cloud's come down on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'carefully' about moving in with Callum. Why carefully?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to move in because I'm scared. I want to move in because I want to. In this picture it'd be both, and I'd hate not knowing which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I'm reacting, not choosing. I'm the sort who waits to see things work. Two years, by the time I've seen it work, it's already here.

S2.say: I'd say I won't believe it until a robot walks up Carrow Fell in sideways rain. She'd say it half joking and expect people to laugh with her.
S2.think: Privately she'd lose her job and her house together, since the cottage is tied to the job. Two years isn't enough to save, rent somewhere and retrain.
S2.do: Stops spending and saves everything at once and raises moving in with her boyfriend. Once it arrives, looks for government support and sells her young dogs while they still have value.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like looking up to see cloud come down on the hill.
S2.quote: Two years, by the time I've seen it work, it's already here.
S2.fieldNote: Her joke hides real fear about losing home and job together. The short timeline clashes with her habit of waiting for proof. A big relationship decision gets forced by money, which troubles her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's enough to get the shock out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for the hills, because hill land is about more than sheep. It's water, birds, peat, walkers. Somebody has to look after it and I'd say that should be the people who know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the shepherd job goes but the land job doesn't, not completely. Somebody has to decide where to block a drain, where to let the heather grow. I could do that. I'd just need the paper to prove it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, keep shepherding, save to six months. Year two, once a couple of others had done it, I'd start a part-time course in land and nature management. I'd keep the dogs going on the side. By year four I'd be applying for ranger or land adviser jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but okay. It's like a hard climb when you can see the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Couldn't AI and robots do land management too, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the measuring. Maybe the digging. But someone has to stand on the hill and talk to the walkers and the grouse people and the water company and make them all agree. I've watched our factor do it. It's people work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the cottage in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move out before I'm pushed. Year three, maybe, into town with Callum, if we're still good. I'd rather leave on my own terms.

S3.say: I'd say the hills need a plan, because hill land means water, birds, peat and walkers as well as sheep. People who know the land should be the ones looking after it.
S3.think: Privately she thinks the shepherd job goes but land management doesn't, because someone has to decide where to block drains and let heather grow. She'd need a qualification to prove she can.
S3.do: Keeps shepherding and saves toward six months in year one, then starts a part-time land and nature management course in year two. Keeps dog training on the side and aims to apply for ranger or land adviser jobs by year four.
S3.feel: Anxious but okay, like a hard climb with the top in sight.
S3.quote: I'd rather leave on my own terms.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her move from shepherd to steward of the land, a step she can picture clearly. She still waits for others to go first, even with a plan. Leaving the tied cottage early is about keeping her dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Moss would be gone by then. Sorry, that's a strange first thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, right, ten years, let's do it properly. Let's train hill people to look after the land and stop pretending it's just about lamb prices. I'd say it at the meetings, steady, not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have time to watch it happen to others first, which is exactly how I like it. I'd see the lowland farms go first, then decide. That's comfortable for me. Maybe too comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shepherding as long as it lasts, probably most of the ten years. I'd do the land management course around year four, at my own pace. Callum and I would probably get a place together and maybe think about kids. I'd breed one more good litter of pups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. There's a sadness about the hill being quiet. But I'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the sadness?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hill without sheep and dogs. Some people would say that's better for the birds, and maybe it is. But a gather on a clear morning, forty dogs whistling across the fell, I'd miss that more than the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years fits me. I can wait and watch and then move. Two years, waiting and watching is the same as doing nothing. That's the difference, really.

S4.say: I'd say ten years means we can do it properly by training hill people to care for the land. She'd say it steadily at meetings, not shouting.
S4.think: Privately she'd have time to watch lowland farms change first, then decide, which suits her. She worries that might make her too comfortable.
S4.do: Keeps shepherding for most of the decade and starts a land management course around year four. Sets up home with her boyfriend, thinks about children and breeds one more litter of pups.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with sadness about the hill going quiet.
S4.quote: Two years, waiting and watching is the same as doing nothing.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture matches how she likes to make decisions, and she knows it. Her sadness is for the working life of the hill, not her pay. Family plans come forward once she feels she has time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose the job and the cottage, and I'm someone who needs to see things work before I move. What would help is a guarantee that people in tied houses get a year to find somewhere, and paid courses in land management for hill workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. I know that sounds daft. But a good dog is ten years of work. What happens to all the working dogs, in the fast one? Nobody's thought about that.

headlineQuote: You can't put a robot on a bog in February.
portrait: Freya Farah is a 27-year-old shepherd who runs 900 ewes on an upland estate with her two dogs, living alone in a cottage that comes with the job and with about four months saved. She's pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, uses AI now and then for forms, and waits for proof before changing anything. She sees the hill as a shelter from robots and worries more about public nature payments than about AI. In the AGI pictures her fear is losing job and home together. With more time she plans to move from shepherding into land and nature management, at her own steady pace.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd lose her job and tied cottage together and doesn't move until she's seen things work.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee that people in tied houses get a year to find a new home, and paid land management courses for hill workers.
